discovery: Opening the window of high-energy neutrino astronomy: discovery of the astrophysical neutrino flux with the IceCube Neutrino Observatory
motivation: Francis Halzen conceived and led the construction of IceCube, a cubic-kilometre neutrino telescope in the Antarctic ice, and turned a decades-old dream into a working observatory. In 2013 IceCube discovered a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, opening a genuinely new window on the Universe. Its real-time alert system then enabled the 2017 coincidence of a neutrino with the flaring blazar TXS 0506+056, followed by evidence for neutrino emission from NGC 1068 and the Galactic plane (2023). These results give the first direct view of hadronic cosmic accelerators, bearing on the century-old problem of cosmic-ray origin. Like gravitational-wave astronomy, neutrino astronomy is now a core pillar of multi-messenger science. It was built on bold detector infrastructure, low-latency alerts and the cooperation of particle physicists with astronomers. Halzen's vision and leadership were decisive at every stage.
